title: Newel Posts
category: NEX Components · Staircase · Structural balustrade component
subcategory: Load-bearing vertical post terminating the handrail run at start · top · landings · turns
summary:
Newel posts are the load-bearing vertical timber (or metal) columns that terminate the handrail run and structurally anchor the balustrade at every start, top, landing, and change of direction of a staircase. They are simultaneously the most structurally critical balustrade component (they carry the entire lateral load of the handrail-and-baluster assembly) and often the most visible design element (a decorative feature newel at the bottom sets the tone of the staircase). Traditional joinery distinguishes several types — starting newel, landing newel, intermediate newel, half-newel — and multiple structural constructions — solid, boxed, veneered, jointed. NEX's proprietary **Nex Newel™ Split Base Design** introduces a stainless-steel divider plate between two timber sections, hiding the joint and delivering a floating-newel visual while remaining fully rigid.

title: Stair Balusters
subcategory: Vertical infill members between newel posts, supporting the handrail and closing the balustrade against fall-through
summary:
Balusters — also called spindles — are the vertical infill members that run between newel posts, supporting the handrail and closing the balustrade to prevent fall-through. They combine two functions inseparably: a **safety infill** governed by the Approved Document K 100mm sphere rule, and an **aesthetic rhythm** that sets much of the visual character of the staircase. Traditional turned timber balusters, square timber balusters, slim metal balusters, wrought iron, and glass panels are all legitimate balustrade infill options — each maps to a Connected Staircase™ tier and to a specific era or design intent. Alongside the newel posts and handrail, balusters complete the three-component balustrade system.

title: Stair Handrails
category: NEX Trade Knowledge · Components · Staircase Components
subcategory: Safety + design feature · continuous or post-to-post
summary:
A stair handrail is the graspable rail running alongside a staircase that provides physical support and guidance for the user. It is both a **safety component** (mandated by Approved Doc K) and a **defining design feature** (the continuous handrail is the single strongest indicator of premium craftsmanship on a staircase). Handrails divide into two systems: **post-to-post** (rail terminates into each newel) and **continuous handrail** (rail passes over intermediate newels as one flowing form). The continuous handrail is a canonical NEX Heritage feature and remains the most difficult specification to execute well.

title: Stair Strings
category: NEX Components · Staircase · Primary structural member
subcategory: Inclined structural beam that carries the treads, risers, and balustrade of a flight
summary:
Strings (also called stringers) are the primary structural members of a staircase — the inclined beams, one on each side of the flight, that carry the treads and risers and to which the balustrade newels are anchored. Strings do the structural work of the entire flight and are the single most load-bearing timber components in the staircase system. Two construction traditions dominate: the **closed string** (NEX branded **NexString™**), in which the treads and risers are housed into the inside face of the string and no tread or riser edge is visible from the side; and the **cut string** (also called open string), in which the top edge of the string is profiled to reveal the tread and riser silhouette. Strings, treads, risers, newels, balusters, and handrails together compose the full flight — Straight, Quarter-Landing, Half-Landing, Winder, Curved, Spiral, or Helical geometries all rest on strings.

title: Ash
category: NEX Trade Knowledge · Materials · Hardwood · European and North American
subcategory: Timber species · reference material · global timber library · sustainability alert
summary:
Ash is the NEX name for two closely related hardwood species commonly specified interchangeably in the UK: **European Ash** (Fraxinus excelsior) and **American White Ash** (Fraxinus americana). Both are pale, straight-grained hardwoods with excellent bending qualities, widely used for staircases, cabinets, flooring, furniture, tool handles, and sports equipment. Ash sits in the premium cost band, generally below oak and walnut. **A significant sustainability crisis is active**: Ash Dieback disease is decimating European Ash across the UK and Europe, and Emerald Ash Borer is devastating North American Ash. UK availability of ash is likely to decline over the next decade.

title: Beech
subcategory: Diffuse-porous temperate hardwood · pale-timber cluster · bentwood specialist
summary:
Beech is a pale, hard, fine-textured diffuse-porous European and North American hardwood renowned for exceptional steam-bending performance (the bentwood chairs of Thonet), stable dimensional behaviour under machining, and hard-wearing properties well-suited to tool handles, workbenches, kitchen worktops, and interior joinery. Two species matter commercially — *Fagus sylvatica* (European Beech) and *Fagus grandifolia* (American Beech) — with European the dominant specification in the UK. Beech has notably poor natural durability outdoors and is prone to greater in-service movement than oak; it is a specialist interior timber, not a general-purpose exterior one.

title: Sapele
subcategory: African tropical hardwood · mahogany-family · interlocked-grain feature timber
summary:
Sapele (*Entandrophragma cylindricum*) is an African tropical hardwood in the mahogany family, prized for its rich reddish-brown colour, distinctive interlocked-grain ribbon-stripe figure, and exceptional dimensional stability once acclimatised. Historically substituted for genuine Mahogany (*Swietenia*) as CITES restrictions tightened on true Mahogany, sapele is itself now CITES Appendix II listed (November 2022), meaning every legitimate order requires CITES permit documentation from range states. FSC-certified sapele is the correct specification. Sapele suits Heritage, Contemporary, and Signature tier staircases, joinery mouldings, and interior architectural work; its interlocked grain is a distinctive design signature but demands careful machining.

title: Ammonia Fuming
subcategory: Chemical colour transformation · tannin-reactive process · Craftsman / dark-oak signature
summary:
Ammonia fuming is a timber colour-transformation process in which timber is exposed to ammonia vapour inside a sealed chamber, causing the tannic acid in the wood to react and darken permanently to a range of amber, chocolate, and near-black tones without applying any surface stain. The process is the canonical technique for the traditional Craftsman, Arts-and-Crafts, and Mission-style dark-oak aesthetic, and it is the correct treatment for producing period-authentic dark oak in Heritage restoration. Fuming works only on tannin-bearing timbers — it is exceptional on European Oak and American White Oak, ineffective on species with low natural tannin (walnut, maple, ash, beech, sapele). Because the process uses concentrated (industrial-strength) ammonia, it requires a purpose-built chamber, strict PPE, and specialist workshop handling — it is not a domestic-site process.

title: Kiln Drying
category: NEX Trade Knowledge · Processes · Timber Handling
summary:
Kiln drying is the controlled reduction of timber moisture content from a green state (typically 40-100% MC) to a specified target (typically 6-12% for interior joinery) using a temperature-controlled and humidity-controlled kiln. It is a prerequisite for almost all interior timber use in the UK. Every NEX timber record references this process; without proper kiln drying, timber moves and joints fail after installation.

title: Moisture Content Verification
category: NEX Trade Knowledge · Processes · Timber Handling · Quality Verification
subcategory: Post-drying quality control · Delivery inspection · Pre-machining verification
summary:
Moisture Content Verification is the workshop practice of measuring the moisture content of timber to confirm it matches specification before machining or installation. It is the standard quality-control step between Kiln Drying and use. Common methods are the resistance moisture meter (workshop standard), the capacitance moisture meter, and the oven-dry method (laboratory reference). Verification is required for premium NEX specifications and prevents costly post-installation movement.
